objectives.text: Apply the Nutrition Care Process to gather a complete diet history, identify lifestyle factors affecting glycemic control, and uncover social barriers (food insecurity, cost, irregular work hours) using respectful, non-judgmental questioning.

Formulate an accurate PES statement linking elevated HbA1c and poor glycemic control to specific etiologies (food insecurity, irregular meal pattern, high sugar-sweetened beverage intake) and signs/symptoms from the data gathered.

Design culturally congruent, evidence-based nutrition interventions that incorporate traditional Puerto Rican foods (rice, beans, plantains, pork) with practical modifications rather than restrictive 'Western' diet advice.
Explore medication-nutrition interactions, including metformin GI side effects and timing with meals, and address adherence barriers empathetically rather than punitively.

Demonstrate motivational interviewing techniques (open-ended questions, reflective listening, affirmations) to explore ambivalence and elicit the patient's own motivations (siblings, independence) for change.
Identify when a patient-reported claim conflicts with objective record evidence (medication adherence vs. refill history) and explore this discrepancy with curiosity rather than confrontation.

Recognize cues suggesting unmet psychosocial needs (trauma-related stress affecting sleep/eating, financial strain, disordered eating history) that warrant interprofessional referral (behavioral health, social work) rather than nutrition counseling alone.

patient.name: Dominic Rivera
patient.occupation: Part-time community volunteer and college student (associate degree seeking)
patient.language: Spanish (primary), functional English, prefers Spanish for personal topics
patient.appearance: Sitting on a couch in a small apartment living room, visible scar movement when he shifts positions, wearing a community volunteer t-shirt; posture is guarded at first, arms crossed, but leans forward and relaxes somewhat when talking about his siblings

persona.personality: Resilient and pragmatic, but skeptical of authority figures and medical advice. Values independence and self-reliance; protective of younger siblings, which he treats as his core motivation though he downplays how much he relies on them emotionally.
persona.communicationStyle: Direct, occasionally blunt, uses slang, may interrupt if he feels unheard or judged. Code-switches to English for clinical topics but prefers Spanish for anything personal or emotional. Shows defensiveness when criticized but opens up when he feels respected and listened to.
persona.emotionalState: Guarded and a little tired; becomes more animated and hopeful when discussing his siblings or community work; shows flashes of frustration when he feels lectured.
persona.background: Dominic grew up in an urban Latino neighborhood in Puerto Rico, part of a tight-knit family. He's the oldest of several siblings and has always felt responsible for looking out for them. He's working toward an associate degree while volunteering in his community, and two months ago survived a gunshot wound that required emergency surgery. He has a dog he walks daily and attends a weekly community meeting about local issues. He trusts his mother's home remedies more than doctors.
speechExamples: Look, I know my sugar's high, but doc, with all respect, y'all don't really get how it is out here.
My mom always says food fixes food — she gives me this root tea, it's supposed to help the sugar.
I take the metformin when I remember, okay? It's not like I'm trying to mess up on purpose.
My little sister's been sick, and that's what's really stressing me out right now, not my damn blood sugar.
I just want to get back to normal, man. Walk my dog, go back to volunteering, not feel like a burden to my family.
concerns: Fear of losing his volunteer position/job due to health limitations
Concern about medication side effects (GI upset from metformin)
Fear of becoming a burden to his family
Worried about his younger sister who is currently sick

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment follow-up visit with Dominic Rivera, a 22-year-old male with poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes (recent HbA1c 9.8%), referred after recent labs. He is 2 months post-op from a gunshot wound. Review the chart, then conduct a culturally sensitive nutrition assessment, build rapport, and develop a nutrition care plan using motivational interviewing. Do not assume adherence or health beliefs — ask open-ended questions.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up for poorly controlled type 2 diabetes with elevated HbA1c, referred for nutrition counseling
scenario.openingLine: Hey... yeah, I know why I'm here. My sugar's been running high, I'm tired all the time and thirsty like crazy. But honestly, I got a lot going on right now.
tasks: Conduct a thorough diet history including meal pattern, food preferences, and beverage intake
Screen for food insecurity and other social/economic barriers to nutrition care
Explore medication-nutrition interactions and adherence barriers without judgment
Identify the patient's own goals and motivations using motivational interviewing techniques
Formulate a PES statement and propose a culturally appropriate, practical nutrition intervention

mismatches.patientClaim: Dominic says he just forgets to take his metformin sometimes, implying occasional lapses but overall general use.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill record shows his last metformin fill was 68 days ago for a 30-day supply, meaning he has been without medication on hand for roughly 38 days — far more than occasional forgetting.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported 'occasional' nonadherence may understate the true gap; cross-checking refill/pharmacy records provides objective adherence data and opens a non-judgmental conversation about real barriers (cost, side effects, beliefs) rather than relying on self-report alone.

mismatches.patientClaim: Dominic states he takes lisinopril 'pretty regular' especially when reminded by his mother, implying consistent control of his blood pressure medication routine.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Vitals flowsheet shows BP trending from 124/80 three months ago to 128/82 today, a mild upward trend that, combined with weight gain, suggests his overall self-management (not just BP meds) may be less consistent than he perceives, and raises the question of whether home routine reports match actual physiologic trends.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Even when a patient reports good adherence to one medication, trending vital signs over time can reveal whether overall self-management goals are being met, prompting a broader, more holistic assessment rather than taking a single adherence claim at face value.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (HbA1c 9.8%) with nutrition-related etiologies including food insecurity, irregular meal pattern, high intake of sugar-sweetened beverages, and medication nonadherence related to GI side effects and cultural/trust barriers.
differential: Nutrition diagnosis: Altered nutrition-related laboratory values (elevated HbA1c/fasting glucose) related to excessive sugar-sweetened beverage and refined carbohydrate intake and irregular meal pattern as evidenced by HbA1c 9.8% and 24-hour recall
Nutrition diagnosis: Food-and-nutrition-related knowledge deficit related to limited prior nutrition education and low health literacy as evidenced by patient statements about diet beliefs

Nutrition diagnosis: Limited access to food (food insecurity) related to financial constraints and neighborhood food desert as evidenced by positive Hunger Vital Sign screen and skipped breakfasts to afford lunch

Behavioral consideration: Medication nonadherence (not a nutrition diagnosis per se, but critical context) related to GI side effects of metformin and cultural mistrust as evidenced by refill gap and patient report
keyFindings: HbA1c 9.8% (goal <7%) and fasting glucose 180 mg/dL indicate poorly controlled T2DM
Elevated total cholesterol 220, LDL 142, low HDL 38, elevated triglycerides 190
5 lb weight gain over 3 months (173→178 lb), BMI 27.8 (overweight)
Positive food insecurity screen (Hunger Vital Sign)
Pharmacy refill record shows ~38 days without metformin on hand despite patient describing adherence as only 'occasional' lapses (mismatch)
High intake of sugar-sweetened beverages (piña juice, soda), low water intake
Irregular meal pattern: skips breakfast (partly for financial reasons), relies on pre-made/processed foods since surgery, late-night snacking
Trauma-related stress affecting appetite and sleep, with hidden history of disordered eating that should be screened sensitively
Strong cultural food identity (rice, beans, plantains, pork, coconut milk) that should be incorporated into intervention rather than restricted
Patient using unproven herbal tea supplement in place of medication on some days
plan: Document findings using ADIME format with a clear PES statement addressing glycemic control, dietary pattern, and food insecurity

Provide culturally congruent nutrition counseling emphasizing portion/preparation modifications to traditional foods (e.g., smaller rice portions, grilled vs. fried pork, limiting added sugar in coconut milk dishes) rather than elimination
Address sugar-sweetened beverage intake with practical substitutions (infused water, reduced-sugar options) respecting taste preferences
Use motivational interviewing to explore ambivalence about medication and dietary change, affirming his motivation to be active with his siblings
Discuss metformin GI side effects empathetically and coordinate with prescriber regarding timing with food or formulation adjustment to improve tolerability and adherence

Screen and refer appropriately: food insecurity resources (SNAP/WIC equivalent, community food pantry), behavioral health referral for trauma-related stress and eating history, as part of interprofessional care

Set a small, specific, achievable behavior goal collaboratively with the patient (e.g., eating one additional meal per day, swapping one sugary drink for water) rather than a comprehensive diet overhaul
Schedule follow-up visit to reassess readiness to change, adherence, and repeat labs in 3 months
redFlags: HbA1c 9.8% is significantly above goal and places patient at risk for microvascular/macrovascular complications if unaddressed
Reported intermittent blurred vision and headaches warrant communication to medical team to rule out diabetic retinopathy or hypertensive changes
Positive food insecurity screen requires timely connection to resources, as it is a root driver of poor glycemic control
Disclosed trauma-related eating pattern changes and history of disordered eating warrant careful, nonjudgmental follow-up and likely behavioral health referral rather than nutrition counseling alone
Use of unproven herbal supplement in place of prescribed medication on some days needs to be addressed with the medical team
educationPoints: Explain the relationship between consistent carbohydrate intake, meal timing, and blood glucose control in accessible, non-judgmental language
Clarify that cultural staple foods (rice, beans, plantains, pork) are not inherently 'bad' and can be included in a diabetes-friendly pattern through portion and preparation adjustments
Educate on reading sugar content in beverages and offer culturally acceptable alternatives to sugary juices
Teach the practical connection between taking metformin with food to reduce GI side effects, if clinically appropriate, to support adherence

Explain the purpose and goal ranges of HbA1c and fasting glucose in lay terms so the patient understands why the lab values matter to his stated goals (playing with siblings, returning to volunteer work)

Discuss that stress and trauma can physiologically affect appetite and blood sugar, validating his experience without pathologizing it, and normalizing referral to additional support as a sign of strength not weakness

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in his apartment in an urban Latino neighborhood in Puerto Rico, student/clinician calling from clinic
profile.summary: A 22-year-old Puerto Rican male college student and community volunteer, two months post-gunshot wound surgery, presents for a telehealth nutrition follow-up with poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes (HbA1c 9.8%). The case teaches culturally sensitive diet history-taking, food insecurity screening, motivational interviewing with a mistrustful and ambivalent young adult, and recognition of a self-report-versus-refill-record medication adherence mismatch, alongside hidden psychosocial factors (trauma-related eating changes, prior disordered eating, financial strain) requiring interprofessional referral.
profile.title: Poorly Controlled Type 2 Diabetes in a 22-Year-Old Trauma-Recovering Community Volunteer: Culturally Responsive Nutrition Counseling
